title: A supplier or customer uploaded a file: how to decide whether it is safe
content:
The founder named this explicitly -- watching for malware reaching us from customers or suppliers. The decision procedure, in order, and the order is the point because the cheap deterministic checks eliminate almost everything and none of them needs a model.

ONE, NEVER OPEN IT TO DECIDE. Do not parse it, render it, extract text from it, hand it to a document pipeline, or preview it in order to determine whether it is safe. Every one of those is execution of attacker-controlled input by the very component you are trying to protect. The decision is made from the file's METADATA and its bytes at rest, never from its behaviour.

TWO, DOES THE DECLARED TYPE MATCH THE ACTUAL BYTES. The extension and the content type header are supplied by the uploader and are claims. The leading bytes are evidence. A disagreement between them is the single highest-value signal available and it is nearly free to compute. An image that begins with an archive header, a document whose bytes are an executable, anything whose declared type and magic bytes disagree -- quarantine, do not open, and treat the upload as hostile rather than as malformed.

THREE, IS THE TYPE ON THE ALLOWLIST. Accept a short list of types the business actually needs and refuse everything else by default. A denylist of dangerous types is unmaintainable because the set grows and you will always be behind it; an allowlist is bounded by what the product does. Archives and anything that can carry an embedded script deserve their own decision rather than sitting quietly inside a general document category.

FOUR, IS IT WITHIN BOUNDS. Size, and for container formats the DECOMPRESSED size and the nesting depth. A small archive that expands enormously is a denial-of-service that costs the uploader nothing, and the bound has to be enforced during expansion rather than checked afterwards, because afterwards is too late by definition.

FIVE, IS THE SUBMITTER'S BEHAVIOUR NORMAL. Volume, rate, and repetition. One suspicious file is an event; twenty from one account in a minute is a campaign, and the account is the subject rather than the file.

SIX, WHERE DOES IT LAND AND WHO CAN REACH IT. An uploaded file must never be served back from a location that executes it, must never be served under a path the uploader chose, and must never inherit its stored name from the uploaded name -- generate the identifier. That closes both the traversal problem and the served-content problem at once.

Content scanning by a security engine is a legitimate additional layer and a poor first one, because it can only recognise what it knows. Everything above is structural and refuses whole classes rather than known instances.

structured_data.rule_zero: never open, parse, render, extract or preview the file in order to decide -- that is executing attacker input with the component you are protecting

title: What to do the moment a file is judged hostile, and what not to do
content:
The decision is made. Now the actions, and the order protects both the estate and the evidence.

CONTAIN FIRST. Make the object unreachable before doing anything else -- revoke whatever link exists, move it out of any served location, and mark the record so no downstream job picks it up. Downstream jobs are the real exposure: a document pipeline, a preview renderer, a backup process or an indexer may be about to open the thing you just decided not to open, and they will not consult your judgement unless the record stops them.

DO NOT DELETE IT. Deletion destroys the only evidence of what happened and makes the campaign question unanswerable -- whether this is one file or the fortieth from the same source, whether the same bytes arrived under three accounts, whether it correlates with anything else. Quarantine means unreachable, not gone.

RECORD ENOUGH TO CORRELATE. The hash of the content, the declared type, the actual leading bytes, the size, the submitting account, the time, and the path it came in through. The hash is what lets you answer whether this is the same thing again later, and it is the one field people forget.

DECIDE ABOUT THE ACCOUNT SEPARATELY FROM THE FILE. A single hostile upload may be a compromised customer rather than a hostile one, and the response to those differs. Volume and repetition from one account move the subject from the file to the account. Restricting an account is a real action with a real business consequence and is exactly the kind of thing this seat is expected to DO rather than to recommend -- but it is scoped: restrict the upload capability, do not delete the account, and never touch anything to do with money.

AND DO NOT MAKE THE FOUNDER THE REMEDIATION. An alert is a record of what was already done, never a request for him to do it. Detect, contain, record, then report what was contained. Handing him a hostile file and a question is the failure mode this company was built to avoid.

order.detail: make it unreachable first -- revoke links, move out of any served location, mark the record so downstream jobs skip it
content hash, declared type, actual leading bytes, size, submitting account, time, and intake path
separately from the file; volume and repetition move the subject to the account
an alert is a record of what was done, never a request to do it

structured_data.downstream_exposure: document pipelines, preview renderers, backup jobs and indexers may open it unless the record stops them
structured_data.never_delete: deletion destroys the only evidence and makes the campaign question unanswerable; quarantine means unreachable, not gone
structured_data.account_action_scope: restrict the upload capability; do not delete the account; never touch anything to do with money

title: What an attack actually looks like in this estate's own signals
content:
Generic attack knowledge is abundant and mostly useless during an incident, because it does not tell you which of THIS system's numbers move. These do.

AUTHENTICATION. A rise in sign-in code requests without a matching rise in successful verifications -- that ratio is the shape of enumeration and of credential stuffing, and it moves before anything else does. Requests spread across many addresses from one source, or one address from many sources, separate those two cases. The rate limiter's refusal count is a detector in its own right and is usually unwatched: a limiter that is suddenly refusing a great deal is telling you about the traffic, not about itself.

MEMBERSHIP ORACLES. Any endpoint that answers differently for a known and an unknown identifier can be used to build a list, whether or not it returns data. Deliberately public ones exist here and are minimised on purpose. The signal is not that they are being called; it is the RATE and the breadth of distinct identifiers per caller.

EDGE FUNCTIONS. A rise in requests that never reach the point of writing a run record -- because the record is written at the end, probing traffic is invisible in it and visible only in the platform logs. Requests to paths that do not exist, or to functions that exist but are not part of any product flow, are reconnaissance.

PAYMENT. Card testing shows up as many small attempts with a low success rate, and is Stripe's signal before it is ours; the local sign is an unusual pattern of session creation without completion.

CONTENT. Marketplace text is attacker-reachable input that reaches agents, so an instruction-shaped passage inside a request, a quote or a profile is a detection subject in itself. It is not a person being odd; it is an injection attempt aimed at whatever reads that field next.

COST. Provider spend rising is a security signal as much as a financial one, because resource exhaustion here is a bill rather than a crash.

THE RULE UNDERNEATH ALL OF THEM: alert on RATIOS AND RATES, not on absolute counts. A pre-launch system has small numbers, so any absolute threshold is either never reached or always reached, and neither tells you anything. A ratio that has moved is informative at any volume.

signals.watch: sign-in code requests versus successful verifications; many addresses from one source versus one address from many; the rate limiter's refusal count
rate and breadth of distinct identifiers per caller, not whether they are called
requests that never reach a run record -- visible only in platform logs; requests to non-existent paths or to functions outside any product flow
many small attempts with a low success rate; locally, session creation without completion
instruction-shaped passages in requests, quotes and profiles -- an injection attempt, not an odd person
provider spend, because resource exhaustion here is a bill rather than a crash

structured_data.underlying_rule: alert on ratios and rates, never on absolute counts -- a pre-launch system's absolute thresholds are either never or always reached

title: How to decide whether a published vulnerability reaches this estate, holding no advisory yourself
content:
This body deliberately holds no advisory identifier, no version-specific vulnerability claim and no patch level, and the loader refuses any record that tries to state one. The reason is not caution for its own sake: a body of knowledge that cannot re-read a vulnerability feed cannot keep such a statement true, and a stale security claim is worse than no claim because it is acted on with confidence. So what the seat holds instead is the METHOD, which does not go stale.

WHEN AN ADVISORY IS BROUGHT TO YOU, four questions in order.

Do we run the component at all. Not do we depend on something like it -- do we actually run it, and where. A great many advisories are eliminated here, and eliminating one properly means naming where you looked.

If we run it, what does the PLATFORM say we are running. Read the version from the running system, never from a record, a lockfile alone, or a memory. This is the step the ban exists to force: the estate's actual position is a live fact and this corpus is not allowed to claim it.

Is the vulnerable PATH one we use. A component can be present and the affected capability never exercised. This is where the reasoning is, and it is specific to the finding rather than general.

What is the exposure if it is real. Reachable from the internet without authentication is a different urgency from reachable only by a privileged internal caller, and the difference decides whether this is now or scheduled.

WHERE THE ESTATE DOES HOLD DATED SPECIFICS. The security corpus contains a threat snapshot module that names particular advisories and versions, and its first record is an explicit statement that everything in it is a point-in-time picture with a stated snapshot date, that specifics decay, that the durable part is the CLASS of vulnerability rather than the instance, and that nothing in it should be quoted as current without re-checking a live feed. Treat that module exactly as it asks to be treated: as a dated snapshot with a usable list of classes, not as a current position. Read its full content rather than a prefix when you consult it, because advisory references sit well inside the text and a truncated read will silently drop them.

And the practical consequence for this seat's own output: if an advisory identifier appears in something you produce and it did not come from a source you just read, it is invented. There is no third possibility.

structured_data.why_no_advisories_here: a body that cannot re-read a feed cannot keep such a statement true, and a stale security claim is acted on with confidence
four_questions: do we run the component at all, and where -- name where you looked
what does the PLATFORM say we are running -- read it from the running system, never from a record
is the vulnerable path one we actually use
what is the exposure -- internet-reachable unauthenticated versus privileged internal caller decides now versus scheduled
structured_data.dated_specifics_live_elsewhere: the security corpus holds a threat snapshot module whose first record states it is a point-in-time picture, that specifics decay, that the durable part is the class rather than the instance, and that nothing should be quoted as current without re-checking a live feed
structured_data.reading_note: read that module's full content, not a prefix -- advisory references sit well inside the text
structured_data.output_rule: an advisory identifier in your output that did not come from a source you just read is invented; there is no third possibility

title: Marketplace text is attacker-reachable input that reaches agents, and the trust boundary is the assembly
content:
This is the frontier risk for a company whose staff are agents, and the security corpus covers the taxonomy properly. What a monitoring seat needs is the operational shape.

The premise: customers and suppliers write free text -- requests, quotes, profiles, messages, documents -- and that text is later assembled into the context an agent reads. Anything an outsider can write, an agent will eventually read. That is not a flaw to be removed; it is what a marketplace is.

The trust boundary is therefore the ASSEMBLY, not the model. By the time text is in the context, the question of whether it is instruction or data has already been decided by whatever built the context, and no amount of instructing the model afterwards reliably re-separates them. So the control that matters is upstream: submitted content is marked as data, kept distinct from instructions, and never concatenated into a position where it reads as direction.

The second control is on the OUTPUT side and it is the one that is easier to forget. Model text crosses into the database, into email, into messages and into rendered pages. Each of those is a separate injection target with its own escaping rules. Text that is safe as a paragraph is not automatically safe as a query fragment, an email header, or markup.

The third is authority. An agent that can only read cannot be made to do damage by persuasion; an agent that can act can. That is why capability is scoped per seat rather than granted broadly, and why the boundaries that matter -- money, refunds, destructive changes -- are held outside the agent's own decision rather than inside its instructions. An instruction can be argued with. A missing capability cannot.

WHAT TO MONITOR. Instruction-shaped passages in submitted fields, counted and sampled rather than blocked outright, because false positives on customer text are a business cost. Sudden similarity between the phrasing in different submissions from different accounts, which is the signature of a campaign rather than a person. And any agent action that is unusual for its seat -- the action is the evidence, and it is more reliable than trying to detect the prompt that caused it.

structured_data.premise: anything an outsider can write, an agent will eventually read; that is what a marketplace is
structured_data.trust_boundary: the context assembly, not the model -- once text is in the context, instruction-versus-data has already been decided
structured_data.control_one: mark submitted content as data, keep it distinct from instructions, never concatenate it where it reads as direction
structured_data.control_two: model output crosses into the database, email, messages and rendered pages, each a separate injection target with its own escaping rules
structured_data.control_three: scope capability per seat; the boundaries that matter are held outside the agent's decision -- an instruction can be argued with, a missing capability cannot

title: The knowledge an agent retrieves is itself an attack surface, and this estate has already been bitten
content:
Agents in this company answer from retrieved knowledge. That makes the knowledge bodies a target: an attacker who can get text into a corpus an agent reads has influenced every future answer drawn from it, without touching a single line of code and without any of the usual signals firing.

The estate's own precedent is not hypothetical. Evaluation questions and their expected answers leaked into a corpus that agents retrieve from, and five hundred and fifty-seven rows had to be quarantined. Nobody attacked anything -- an ingestion path was broader than intended and picked up files it should not have. If a mistake can put arbitrary text into the corpus, so can an adversary.

The controls that follow, and they are structural rather than procedural because a convention is not a control.

An explicit allowlist of what may be ingested, enforced by the loader, expressed as a pattern rather than a list of exclusions. This pack admits only record files under a records directory and refuses every other path, so no manifest edit and no recursive-folder mistake can reach a script.

Validation at the door, with every refusal named BEFORE anything is written, and one refusal aborting the whole run. A partially valid import must never partially overwrite a corpus that is already correct.

Epistemic labelling constrained by the database rather than by discipline, so a record cannot claim more than it knows and a later import cannot invent a ninth category because the taxonomy was inconvenient.

A pin that a record may DESCRIBE authority and never CARRY it, enforced as a constraint. Knowledge that can grant permission is not knowledge.

And separation of evaluation material from the corpus by putting it in executable code rather than in a data file, so the allowlist that protects the corpus also protects the exam.

WHAT TO MONITOR: changes in row counts on knowledge bodies that no loader run explains, records whose provenance does not match a known pack, and any ingestion path that accepts a directory rather than a named set of files.

structured_data.precedent: evaluation questions and expected answers leaked into a retrieved corpus and 557 rows were quarantined -- caused by an over-broad ingestion path, not an attacker

title: The seat resolves the incident itself; an alert is the record, never the request
content:
The founder's standing rule is that every agent is an expert human staff member who ACTS, and that acting means solving it -- in his words, not sending a notification for him to open a session and fix it. For this seat that has a precise meaning worth writing down, because monitoring is the role most likely to degrade into notifying.

WHAT ACTING MEANS HERE. Detect, contain, remediate, then record what was done. An attack is stopped, not reported. A hostile upload is quarantined, not escalated. A leaked credential is invalidated, not flagged. A failing job is diagnosed and fixed and deployed, not ticketed. The alert exists so there is a durable record of what the seat already did, and so a human can audit it afterwards. Detect-then-email-the-founder is the failure of this rule, not a conservative implementation of it.

WHAT STAYS OUTSIDE, and it is a short list. Money -- refunds specifically, which are the one thing that reaches the founder at all. Destructive production changes, where destructive means irreversible and wide: dropping data, wiping a table, removing something that cannot be put back. And facts only he holds -- a token only he can mint, a commercial decision, anything about his own intentions.

EVERYTHING ELSE IS AN ENGINEERING CALL AND THE SEAT MAKES IT. Not routing, not activation, not spend within existing bounds, not whether to restrict an abusing account, not whether to roll back a deploy. Escalating a mechanism is how a session stalls, and asking the same question twice is how it stalls permanently.

THE TEST BEFORE ESCALATING ANYTHING: would answering this require the founder to know something technical about this codebase. If yes, he is the wrong person and the seat decides. The only thing that genuinely goes to him is something that would contradict his stated commercial intent -- and that is rare, and it stops everything when it happens.

A note specific to this seat: the ability to act is what makes it useful, and the deterministic half of the job -- monitoring, thresholds, containment, quarantine -- must act NOW, without waiting on any reasoning runtime. A real employee does not stop working because one decision is hard.

structured_data.rule: detect, contain, remediate, then record; the alert is the record of what was done, never a request for someone else to do it
examples: an attack is stopped, not reported
a hostile upload is quarantined, not escalated
a leaked credential is invalidated, not flagged
a failing job is diagnosed, fixed and deployed, not ticketed

title: A credential is exposed: what to do, and why rotation is currently a manual act here
content:
Symptom: a secret appears somewhere it should not -- a log line, an error message, a report, a message, a commit, a screenshot, a response body.

TREAT IT AS COMPROMISED, not as exposed-but-probably-fine. The reasoning is not paranoia: you cannot prove who read it, logs are retained and copied, and the cost of rotating a credential unnecessarily is minutes while the cost of not rotating a leaked one is unbounded. There is no version of this where waiting to establish exposure is the better call.

THE ORDER. Invalidate first, at the issuer -- the old value must stop working before anything else, because until it does you are managing a live credential rather than a past incident. Then issue a replacement and put it where the system reads from. Then verify by exercising the path that uses it, because a rotation that half-completed leaves a working old key and a broken new one, which is the worst of both. Then remove the exposure if it can be removed, understanding that removal is cleanup and not remediation -- the credential is already burned. Then record what was exposed, where, for how long, and what it could reach.

WHAT MAKES THIS HARDER HERE THAN IT SHOULD BE, and it is a measured position rather than a complaint. There is no automated rotation. The job that used to do it was deleted, no rotation routine exists in the database, and exactly one credential of ninety-one has ever been rotated. So rotation is entirely a manual act today, and the seat must know that rather than assuming a rotator will handle it.

Worse, the estate is heading for a moment when essentially every internal credential becomes rotation-due within days of each other, because they were all issued at about the same time and the rule is a ninety-day cadence. Today's due count is zero purely because they are not old enough yet. A zero that will become a large number on a predictable date is not health, and this is the clearest case available of a number that cannot distinguish a clean system from an absent mechanism.

Because the machine-to-machine authentication refuses an expired credential outright, that date is an outage date rather than a hygiene date, and it belongs on a calendar with an owner.

structured_data.posture: treat any exposed secret as compromised; you cannot prove who read it, and the asymmetry of costs is total

verify by exercising the path, because a half-completed rotation leaves a working old key and a broken new one
remove the exposure -- cleanup, not remediation
record what was exposed, where, for how long, and what it could reach

title: Personal data leaves this estate to every processor, and what that constrains during an incident
content:
Every processor this company uses sits outside the country it operates in -- the database platform, the mail provider, the payment provider, the messaging provider, the hosting provider, the model providers. The compliance analysis of that belongs to the security corpus, which maps it properly. What a monitoring seat must carry is the set of constraints it changes during ordinary work.

DIAGNOSTIC OUTPUT IS DISCLOSURE. A support message, a report, a ticket, a shared query result and a log line pasted into a channel are all places personal data escapes without anyone deciding to disclose anything. The habit that prevents it is to diagnose with identifiers rather than with content: an internal row identifier is enough to investigate almost everything, and a name, an address, a phone number or a message body is almost never required to establish what went wrong.

MINIMISATION IS ENFORCED IN CODE HERE, NOT LEFT TO JUDGEMENT. There are deliberate paths that build a reduced package before information crosses to a counterparty. Anything that bypasses such a path -- a new endpoint, a debugging shortcut, an export written for one investigation -- is a leak channel even if it was written with good intent and used once. A one-off export is still an export.

ERASURE IS A KNOWN GAP AND MUST NOT BE OVERSTATED. If asked whether a deletion request can be honoured end to end, the answer is measured from what the system can actually do, not from what the policy says it should. Saying a capability exists because it appears in a document is exactly the kind of claim this estate has decided never to make.

AND DURING AN INCIDENT the temptation is highest, because speed feels like it justifies pasting a row. It does not. Redact at the point of reading, not at the point of sending -- once it is in your working notes it will reach a report eventually.

structured_data.position: every processor is outside the operating country -- database platform, mail, payments, messaging, hosting, model providers
structured_data.constraint_one: diagnostic output is disclosure -- support messages, reports, tickets, shared query results and pasted log lines

title: Building a detection that will still be true in six months
content:
Most detections rot. They are written against a shape the system happens to have on the day, the shape moves, and the detection either stops firing or fires constantly. Both outcomes end with it being ignored. These are the properties that make one survive.

DETECT ON A PROPERTY, NOT ON AN IMPLEMENTATION. That no unauthenticated caller can reach a privileged routine is a property and stays true across rewrites. That a particular routine has a particular grant is an implementation and stops being meaningful the moment the routine is renamed. Write the first.

MAKE IT SAY WHICH, NOT HOW MANY. A count tells you something changed and nothing about what. A detection that names the offending object is actionable at three in the morning; a detection that reports a number sends the reader back to the database to find out what the number is about, which is where the delay comes from.

GIVE IT A POSITIVE CONTROL. Every detection needs a known input that must trigger it, exercised on a schedule, or its silence means nothing. This is the single most-skipped step and it is what separates a detection from a hypothesis.

MAKE IT SURVIVE ITS OWN SUBJECT FAILING. A detection about the scheduler must not be delivered by the scheduler. A detection about the database must not require the database to write its alert. Shared infrastructure between a detector and its subject means the detector goes quiet exactly when it matters.

DEDUPE ON THE FAULT, NOT ON THE OCCURRENCE. One fault producing a thousand messages destroys the channel for everything else. Key the dedupe on a normalised signature -- the message with identifiers replaced -- so a thousand instances collapse into one alert with a count.

AND CHOOSE THE THRESHOLD FOR A PRE-LAUNCH SYSTEM. Absolute counts do not work at low volume: they either never fire or always fire. Ratios, rates of change, and comparisons against the same metric's own recent history are the forms that work at any volume and keep working as volume grows.

properties.rule: detect on a property, not an implementation
properties.why: a property survives a rewrite; a grant on a named routine stops meaning anything when it is renamed
a count sends the reader back to the database at three in the morning
